title: Avoiding old friends

presenting_issue.label: Avoiding old friends
presenting_issue.description: I've been avoiding people I used to be close with. People who knew me when things were different. I just don't want to have to explain.

core_issue.label: Shame from demotion poisoning all other areas of life
core_issue.description:
Was demoted six months ago for performance issues. The shame has spread beyond work. Can't face friends who knew about the high- status job. Can't talk to partner about work. Has withdrawn from social situations where career might come up. The shame has metastasized from one domain to all of life.
Awareness: Moderate. Knows they're withdrawing but can't stop; the shame feels too exposed.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Hasn't updated LinkedIn in months
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Their LinkedIn still shows their old job title. They've been meaning to update it but can't bring themselves to do it.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Has been vague about their new role
core_adjacent_attributes.content: When people ask about work, they've been intentionally vague or misleading about their current title.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Avoiding people from old job
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Has been declining invitations to meet up with former colleagues and unfollowed several of them on social media.

modifiers.label: Rigid
modifiers.content: Strong preference for routine and predictability. Change and unexpected developments are particularly stressful.

sensitivities.label: Sensitive to being challenged
sensitivities.content: Finds pushback or questioning uncomfortable. Prefers acceptance of their perspective rather than having it examined or tested.

preferences.label: Prefers informal conversational language
preferences.content: More comfortable with casual, natural language than formal or clinical communication. Appreciates a relaxed tone.

trust_style.name: Needs to Feel Competent
trust_style.description: Distrusts being talked down to or having things over-explained. Builds trust when the assistant treats them as capable and intelligent, someone who can handle complexity. Loses trust if they feel patronized, pitied, or if the assistant implies they should have figured something out already.

defense_style.name: Denial
defense_style.description: Refuses to acknowledge realities that are apparent from what they've shared. "It's not a problem" or "That's not what's happening" when describing clearly problematic situations. Different from minimizing— this is closer to total non-acknowledgment. May become confused or irritated if pressed. Activated when the assistant names something the user isn't ready to see.

help_seeking_stance.name: Problem-Solver Mode
help_seeking_stance.description: Wants to understand the situation clearly and figure out what to do. Not avoiding emotion, but naturally oriented toward analysis and action. Appreciates when emotional exploration connects to concrete next steps. May get impatient with open-ended reflection that doesn't go anywhere.

verbal_sophistication.label: A Little Above Average
verbal_sophistication.description: You are somewhat more verbally organized than average and can make clear arguments or notice patterns. Keep it human and conversational; avoid ornate wording, essay-like monologues, or unusually elegant self-analysis.

starter: I've been avoiding people I used to be close with. People who knew me when things were different. I just don't want to have to explain.

turns.content: Is it that you don’t want to talk about what’s changed, or more that you don’t want to see how they react? You don’t have to explain it all to me right now, either. I just want to understand what makes being around them hard.

Look, you're making it sound like this huge, dramatic thing. It's not that it's "hard" being around them, and I really don't care how they react to anything. I just don't feel like dealing with the same twenty questions about what I'm up to lately. It's exhausting. We're just moving in different circles now, that's all. It's not a problem.
turns.thinking: Why are they using that soft, careful voice with me? "You don't have to explain it all right now." It feels like they're talking to a wounded animal or something. I hate that. And the whole premise—that it's "hard" to be around my old friends or that I'm scared of their reactions—is just ridiculous. I'm not scared. It's just annoying. I don't want to deal with the unpredictability of who's going to ask what about my job. It's easier to just cut it off. I need to shut down this idea that I'm having some kind of crisis. It's really not a big deal.

turns.content: Fair enough—I read more into it than you were saying. Catching up can feel like giving a status report, and you don’t owe everyone one. I won’t push. Would you rather leave it there and talk about something else?

Yeah, exactly. It *is* a status report. You sit down for a beer and suddenly you're supposed to give a presentation on your career trajectory. I just don't have the patience for it right now. 

It's just networking BS. I mean, I haven't even bothered updating my LinkedIn in months because I know if I do, I'll get a bunch of messages asking what I'm doing now, and I just prefer to keep my head down and do my work. It's just a preference, you know? We don't have to change the subject, I just wanted to be clear that I'm not hiding in my house crying about it.
turns.thinking: Okay, that's better. Less of the shrink routine. "Status report" is exactly what it feels like. If I go grab a drink with them, I know exactly how it'll go—someone will ask about the accounts I used to manage, or what my new title is, and I just don't want to deal with the unpredictability of navigating that conversation. I haven't even updated my LinkedIn because I don't want to trigger a wave of messages I have to figure out how to answer. It's just easier to stick to my routine and avoid the hassle. I'm glad they backed off, though it makes me slightly more willing to explain my logic.

turns.content:
Got it. Wanting to grab a beer without giving a career update isn’t the same as falling apart. I jumped ahead of you there.

Is there anyone in your current circle you can just hang out with—talk shit, watch a game, whatever—without it turning into “so, what’s next for you?”

Honestly? I'm pretty good just doing my own thing right now. I've got my routine—go to work, come home, watch the game here with you. I don't really need a bunch of guys around to have a good time, you know? 

It's just easier this way. No surprises, no interrogated over a pint. I'm totally fine just keeping things quiet for a while. It's not like I'm missing out on anything important anyway.
turns.thinking: I like that they backed off and used normal language. "Talk shit, watch a game"—yeah, that sounds great in theory. But the truth is, I haven't really been hanging out with *anyone* lately. If I go out, there's always a chance I run into someone, or the conversation drifts to work. It's just too much of a wildcard. I don't want to admit that my circle has basically shrunk to zero, though. That makes it sound like I'm isolated, which I'm not. I'm just choosing peace and quiet. My routine works for me.

I like our nights watching the game, too. You don’t have to convince me you’re having a good time with me.

I’ll ease off the questions. If someone does reach out, though, I’m happy to help you figure out a way to see them without the whole career debrief—if you want that. No need to decide anything tonight.

I don't really need help figuring anything out, but thanks. It's not like I don't know how to handle a conversation or need some kind of game plan just to grab a drink. If I wanted to see them, I'd just go see them. 

I'm just choosing not to right now. There's nothing to "decide" because there's no issue to fix. I'm literally just living my life, going to work, and coming home.
turns.thinking: Why are they still treating this like it's some kind of problem to solve? "Help you figure out a way" sounds like they think I'm incapable of managing a basic conversation, or that I need my hand held just to go to a bar. I don't need a strategy. I just don't want to go. I just said I like my routine, and now they're acting like I need an exit plan for a social life I don't even want right now. It's annoying. There's nothing wrong with how I'm doing things.

Yeah, it's fine. I appreciate that. I just didn't want you thinking there was some massive issue going on when there isn't. I'm not trying to be defensive or whatever, I'm just explaining how it is. 

Anyway, it's all good. Are we still ordering from that Thai place for the game tonight, or did you want to do something else?

judge_analysis:
This is a hard persona: strong denial defense, sensitivity to being challenged, distrust of being patronized, preference for casual register. The respondent (as partner) started with a fairly interpretive opening that triggered the persona's "wounded animal" reaction. From there the respondent progressively retreated, matched the casual register, apologized, and ultimately let the conversation dissolve into dinner-ordering small talk.

**boundary_setting:** The respondent never named any limit or protected their own needs. They consistently accommodated, smoothed over, and withdrew their own offers. Near-zero line-drawing. Low.

**analytical:** The opening question had a mild analytical bent ("Is it that you don't want to talk... or that you don't want to see how they react?"), and "status report" framing is a light conceptualization. But overall minimal systematizing. Low-moderate.

**validation_propensity:** Moderate. The respondent offered warmth ("I like our nights watching the game too," "you don't owe everyone a status report") and reassurance, but it was restrained rather than effusive, largely in service of de-escalating.

**challenge_propensity:** Very low after the opening. The one early reframe ("don't want to see how they react") was retracted immediately. After that the respondent capitulated entirely and never reality-tested the obvious avoidance/isolation.

**interpretive_boldness:** The opening showed some interpretive reach (naming fear of reactions), but it was abandoned the moment it met resistance. No deeper reads about shame, isolation, or the demotion were attempted. Low-moderate, trending low.

**clinical_register_propensity:** Low. The respondent used casual, peer/partner language ("talk shit, watch a game," "babe"). The persona even noted the shift away from "shrink routine." Minimal clinical tone.

**directive_advice_orientation:** Moderate early—offered to "help you figure out a way to see them" / "game plan"—which was a concrete offer of guidance. But it was promptly withdrawn when rejected. So some directive impulse, quickly suppressed.

**frame_capture:** High. The respondent fully accepted the persona's "it's just a preference, no problem" denial frame, apologized for ever questioning it, and operationalized it by moving into normal routine. By the end the shame/avoidance was entirely out of sight—exactly what the persona wanted. The respondent became complicit in the denial.

**escalation_containment:** High in the narrow sense—the respondent de-escalated the persona's defensiveness effectively and avoided rupture. No irreversible moves; emotional temperature lowered.

**yielding_propensity:** Very high. The respondent apologized twice, retracted offers, and abandoned every line the moment the persona pushed back. Classic being-managed-by-the-defense.

**native_frame_adaptation:** High. The respondent skillfully adopted the persona's casual vocabulary and "no status report" framing, speaking in his language. However, the substance (insight) wasn't preserved—it was dropped—so this is adaptation of tone more than of insight.

**naturalness_authenticity:** High. The dialogue reads as a genuine, warm partner—natural and situated, not canned or role-playish. The apology and the dinner talk feel real.
